title: Bhooth Bangla Hits Netflix Thursday. The Diaspora Can Finally Stop Asking.
excerpt: Akshay Kumar and Priyadarshan's ₹264 crore horror comedy — the reunion that made Bollywood believe in ghosts again — arrives on Netflix June 12. Here's why it's worth the wait.
body:
The countdown is over.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=XW1RkKiRnsg

Bhooth Bangla, the horror comedy that had Indian audiences howling in theatres for nearly six weeks, drops on Netflix this Thursday, June 12. For the diaspora — who've been watching trailers on loop and begging NRI cousins for spoilers — the wait is finally, mercifully done. This release is particularly significant for NRIs, as it allows them to reconnect with their roots and enjoy a piece of contemporary Indian cinema from the comfort of their homes.

And what a wait it's been. Directed by Priyadarshan and starring Akshay Kumar in peak chaos mode, Bhooth Bangla has grossed a staggering ₹264 crore worldwide against a production budget of ₹120 crore. It's not just a hit. It's a full-blown vindication — of Akshay's comic instincts, of Priyadarshan's mastery over the genre, and of the fact that Bollywood horror comedies, done right, can still pack houses. This success also reflects the growing appetite for Indian films among global audiences, including those in the US, UK, and Canada, where many NRIs are eager to support and celebrate their cinematic heritage.

The premise is classic Priyadarshan mischief: Arjun (Akshay) inherits a crumbling ancestral palace in a village called Mangalpur after his mother's death. He's a London NRI who doesn't believe in ghosts, obviously. He decides to host his sister's wedding at the palace, because what could possibly go wrong? What follows is a terrifying local legend about a demonic spirit called Vadhusur — said to target newlywed brides — and an entire village trembling under its curse for generations.

If this sounds like Bhool Bhulaiyaa territory, you're not wrong. But Bhooth Bangla leans harder into the horror. The scares are legitimate. The palace interiors are gorgeously creepy — all cracked chandeliers, dust-draped corridors, and shadows that move when they shouldn't. Priyadarshan, who spent years making Malayalam cinema's finest thrillers before pivoting to Hindi comedy, knows exactly when to make you laugh and when to make you grip the armrest.

The Cast Is Stacked

The real pleasure of Bhooth Bangla is watching its ensemble work. Tabu brings her signature intensity to a role that pivots between warmth and menace. Paresh Rawal is in vintage form — his timing remains surgical even after four decades. Rajpal Yadav delivers the kind of physical comedy that only he can, the kind where you laugh so hard you forget to breathe. And Wamiqa Gabbi, who's been quietly building one of the most impressive filmographies in Indian cinema, holds her own against every heavyweight on screen.

But this is Akshay's show. He hasn't been this loose, this playful, this fun in years. There's a sequence in the second half involving a possessed mirror and a very confused priest that might be the single funniest five minutes in Bollywood this year. The internet has already turned it into a meme. Now you'll finally get to see it in context.

"This is the kind of cinema I fell in love with making. Pure entertainment, no pretension." — Priyadarshan, in a recent interview

The Business Was Brilliant Before a Single Ticket Sold

Here's the number that should make every producer in Mumbai sit up: ₹105 crore was recovered before the film even released. Netflix paid a reported ₹60 crore for digital rights. Zee Cinema secured satellite rights for ₹25 crore. Zee Music Company picked up the music for ₹10 crore. That's 87.5% of the budget covered by non-theatrical revenue alone.

The theatrical run was pure profit. Opening weekend crossed ₹65 crore. The film held remarkably well on weekdays, fuelled by family audiences and repeat viewings. By the time it wound down, the worldwide gross had settled at ₹264 crore — comfortably placing it as the third highest-grossing Bollywood film of 2026 behind Dhurandhar 2 and Border 2. This financial success not only boosts the Indian film industry but also enhances the prospects for future projects that cater to the diaspora, who are keen to see their stories represented on screen.

Where to Watch

Netflix, globally, from June 12, 2026. The film will be available in Hindi, Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, and Malayalam — the full dubbed slate. For NRIs in the US, UK, Canada, and the Gulf, this is the one to queue up Thursday night. Make popcorn. Turn the lights off. And maybe keep someone brave nearby.

The Akshay-Priyadarshan pairing has produced some of Indian cinema's most beloved comedies — Hera Pheri, Garam Masala, Bhool Bhulaiyaa, Bhagam Bhag. Each one is a classic in its own right, rewatched endlessly by desi families on lazy Sundays. Bhooth Bangla belongs in that conversation. It's not reinventing the wheel. It's reminding you why the wheel was invented.

Thursday. Netflix. Don't be late.
